content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
This paper proposes to tackle many tasks including among others lifelong learning or transfer learning. To do so, they propose to perform at the feature level an alpha blending between a fixed pretrained representation and a learnable (possibly smaller) network. Such a design allows to avoid catastrophic forgetting by construction and represents a tweakable middle point between a feature extractor and a fully finetuneable network.

I am strongly leaning towards rejection. This paper provides numerous experiments but this should not replace novelty or presenting as novel something already present several times in the literature. For example, the proposed method does not differ much from "Progressive Neural Networks" by Rusu et al. if you switch off their lateral connections. 

Furthermore, several network adaptations papers are missing from the references and also present themselves as tweakable middle points between feature extractor and  a fully finetuneable network. Among others: "Universal representations: The missing link between faces, text, planktons, and cat breeds" by Bilen et al., "Incremental Learning Through Deep Adaptation" by Rosenfeld et al. or "Efficient parametrization of multi-domain deep neural networks" by Rebuffi et al. The latter also proposing an additive adaptation all along the network which preserve the original filters for the original task.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
We agree that there is a connection between side-tuning and Rusu et al. Both are additive approaches, but side-tuning is significantly simpler than PNNs (no lateral connections). Crucially, we show (Figs  20,21,22,23,24) that the lateral connections are unnecessary and do not generally offer an improvement over the simpler approach. We believe that a simpler method should be preferable to complex ones. 

We view the relationship between side-tuning and PNNs as a comparison between late fusion and distributed fusion. We found (Fig 25,26,27,28) that late fusion performs better than early fusion and is comparable to (if not better than) distributed fusion. 

Importantly, both early and distributed fusion require knowledge of how the features are computed. Late fusion (doing away with lateral connections) eliminates this dependence on the architecture of the base network. As Fig 29 shows, side-tuning can be used successfully even with nonparameteric methods for extracting features (an approach used by residual RL [Johannink et al., 2018; Silver et al., 2018]), while PNNs could not be applied. 

1. Missing references present themselves as tweakable middle points between feature extractor and a fully finetuneable network. 
Thank you for bringing these papers to our attention. They are certainly relevant and we will cite them.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper proposed a novel lifelong learning approach, called side-tuning. The idea of side-tuning is that they firstly have a fixed base network and when a new task arrived, they learn the task with a smaller network which transferred the adaptive knowledge from large base network while freezing  it. It can get fine-tune strength without catastrophic forgetting problem.

The approach looks practical that they only train a smaller side-network for new tasks. But the proposed model might have several crucial weakness. 

- It is extremely dependent to the base (pretrained) model. When the base knowledge will be largely different to the arriving tasks, it looks hard to appropriately train the model.

- There is no knowledge transfer among arriving tasks. N side networks can not communicate among them which means they can not manage the redundancy problem among side networks.

- There is a few of ablation study. Why does the model requires to element-wise combination among base parameters and side parameters? It seems that the architectural choice of the model and hyperparameter selection procedure is heuristic.

- Even the model requires less number of 'trainable' parameters, the machine inevitably requires to memorize not only side-network parameters but also base network parameters. Then, in my understanding, the authors are required to compute the total capacity as addition of them, not only with trainable ones.

- Also, the idea looks quite similar to piggyback, or Progressive neural networks that both approach kept the parameters of base network intact. The authors also require to compare with them.

Mallya, Arun, Dillon Davis, and Svetlana Lazebnik. "Piggyback: Adapting a single network to multiple tasks by learning to mask weights." Proceedings of the European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV). 2018.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
Similar to our response for reviewer 2, we will try to address these concerns point-by-point. We have added in comparisons with other additive approaches and find that side-tuning performs as well or better while being significantly simpler. Specifically, side-tuning performs similarly to PNNs, and outperforms PSP which outperforms Piggyback, 

1.It is extremely dependent to the base(pretrained)model.
It is true that the base model must be somehow related and useful for training the arriving tasks - this is a fundamental general assumption in transfer and lifelong learning. We show in Figs 8c, 8d, 9b that side-tuning is able to ignore the base model and learn from scratch if the base model is not useful. 

2.There is no knowledge transfer among arriving tasks. N side networks can not communicate among them which means they can not manage the redundancy problem among side networks.
This is a good point, and therefore this performance should be considered a lower bound on the performance of side-tuning with more parameters. Still, as we show in Fig 7 (right), this basic approach performs as well or better than other approaches that use such information. 

3. Why does the model requires to element-wise combination among base parameters and side parameters?
We use element-wise combination of the base outputs and side outputs because it is simple to implement and analyze, and it works. We compare to alternative combining operators in Figs 6 (right), 20.

4. The agent must memorize not only side-network parameters but also base network parameters.
We generally agree, and we included those parameters in the total count.

5. Comparisons with Piggyback and PNNs.
Please see response 2 to reviewer 2, and Figs 20,21,22,23,24.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper studies continual learning. Fine-tuning from previous task will make the network forget previous knowledge, but directly using features from previous tasks’ network will cause underfitting. This paper proposes a method that is in the middle of fine-tuning and using fixed feature. A new small network is added to the architecture to help the training of new task. The method is evaluated on several datasets. This paper proposes interesting insight but the contribution of the proposed method is very limited.

Comments
1.The setting in this paper is not a rigorous continual learning setting. Continual learning setting require model not to incrementally grow with task number. The novelty of keep all previous model and merely add new network for every task is very limited. 
2.The novelty of the proposed model is very limited. There are several works that proposed more advanced idea than this work such as [A] and [B]. The latter also proposed a method that avoid keeping all previous model in evaluation.
3.The paper argue that the proposed method needs to train only smaller amounts of parameters for each task, but there are several works on this subject as [C]. Please conclude these methods in related works and compare with them.
4.If the architectures of base model and side model are different, how to combine the features from these two networks? 
5.What is Side-tune (R) in Table 5? Why it outperforms Side-tune for a large margin?
6.What is the relationship between the scale of side networks and the difficulties of tasks? How to make sure the architecture that to be used for a certain task? 
7.There is no need to arrange many unchanged images in Figure 5 that takes up much space in the main body of the paper.
From above reasons, I vote for rejecting this paper.

[A] Rusu, Andrei A., et al. "Progressive neural networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1606.04671 (2016).
[B] Flennerhag, Sebastian, et al. "Transferring knowledge across learning processes." arXiv preprint arXiv:1812.01054 (2018).
[C] Rosenfeld, Amir, and John K. Tsotsos. "Incremental learning through deep adaptation." IEEE transactions on pattern analysis and machine intelligence (2018).

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
We will try to address these concerns point-by-point. Overall, we have added in comparisons with other additive approaches and find that side-tuning performs as well or better while being significantly simpler. Specifically, side-tuning performs similarly to PNNs, and outperforms PSP which outperforms Piggyback, 

1. Continual learning setting require model not to incrementally grow with task number. 
A number of alternative methods (EWC, PSP, Piggyback, PNNs, as well as [B] and [C] cited in the initial review) all add parameters in some way--either as regularization constraints or as parameters used during the forward pass.


2. Several works that proposed more advanced idea than this work such as[A]and[B].
We agree that PNNs [A] are a valuable baseline and have added in comparisons in Figs 20,21,22,23,24. The results suggest that side-tuning is significantly simpler than the alternative approaches while offering similar or better performance and side-tuning can be applied in a larger variety of problems (e.g. Fig 29).  We argue that more complex methods should offer demonstrable improvements over the simpler side-tuning approach. The results in Fig 6 suggest that much of the benefits of these alternative methods stem from leaving the base fixed and adding parameters, which is actually one of the main points of the paper.

3.Contrast with methods such as [C].
Please see the response for 2 for a comparison to common additive approaches. Some of the works we compare to (e.g. PSP)  also compare against other methods (e.g. Piggyback). Generally, existing additive approaches are architecture dependent and requiring knowledge about the inner workings of the base model. When the base model is not a neural network, many of these approaches could not be used (though side-tuning can, see Fig 29).

4.If the architectures of base model and side model are different, how to combine the features from these two networks? 
One of the advantages of side-tuning is that as long as the representations are the same shape, side-tuning can be applied while other approaches (PNNs) require making design choices. As shown in Fig 21, those methods can be extremely sensitive to such choices. 

5.What is Side-tune(R)in Table 5? Why it outperforms Side-tune for a large margin?
Side-tune(R) is our method if you use a small network for the base model and a large network for the side model (R for reversed). We include it for comparison to Independent. 

6.What is the relationship between the scale of side networks and the difficulties of tasks?
The scale of the side networks should correspond to the difficulty of the task, but computationally choosing the architecture is outside of the scope of this paper. Indeed, that is one of the primary concerns of subfields such as Neural Architecture Search. 

7.There is no need to arrange many unchanged images in Figure 5 that takes up much space in the main body of the paper.
Thanks for the suggestion--we will update the final paper accordingly.

content.title: Response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their constructive comments. We have revised the paper as suggested by the reviewers, and summarize the major changes as follows:

1. Added in experimental comparisons to existing additive learning approaches, such as Progressive Neural Networks (PNNs). The results suggest that sidetuning, is significantly simpler than alternative approaches, offers similar or better performance, and can be applied on a larger variety of problems. We show supportive results in Figs 20, 21, 22, 23, 24.

2. Experiments in domains where architecture-dependent approaches cannot be used, but side-tuning can.

3. Discussion to existing related work (will be done). In particular, existing additive approaches. Sidetuning takes this family of complex network adaptation methods and captures a small yet core component of these methods that makes them work.

content.title: Training on residuals is not new
content.comment:
The main idea of the paper is to train a secondary model on the difference between a target and predictions of a primary model.  This is a very old idea as it is the root of boosting.

More recently it has been used successfully in machine learning competitions, see for instance:

https://www.kaggle.com/c/web-traffic-time-series-forecasting/discussion/39395

https://www.kaggle.com/c/champs-scalar-coupling/discussion/106421

See also how others reused the idea and pushed it further:

https://twitter.com/senkin13/status/1209250177187336194

replying_to: Replying to Training on residuals is not new
display_title: The simple approach is yielding comparable or better results than more sophisticated techniques

content.title: The simple approach is yielding comparable or better results than more sophisticated techniques
content.comment:
Short answer: sure, the concept of adapting an approximator using lightweight conditioned secondary approximators is indeed very basic and extensively used before as one would expect (notably earlier than the posted kaggle and Twitter references). That’s not the primary point of this paper. The point is that: this simple concept is yielding comparable or better results than more sophisticated approaches for adapting neural networks, hence the study in our paper.  

Long answer: In addition, there are certain conceptual differences with boosting: this paper proposes a method for transfer+lifelong learning that trains a secondary neural network for the task at hand. The output from the secondary model is added to that of the primary model. Importantly, the primary model can come from any source or could be trained for a different task entirely. This differs from boosting in that the primary and secondary models have distinct and/or unrelated training objectives.

For a discussion of this method versus other residual learning methods (including boosting and other approaches that use primary and secondary models) see the related work--specifically sections ‘residual learning’, ‘network adaptation’, and ‘incremental learning’. There are also empirical comparisons (including an experiment specifically comparing the proposed method against boosting) that suggest the proposed method is not working via a boosting mechanism. The extensive experimental studies we performed demonstrated this simple baselined based on an intuitive and straghwoard concept is worth consideration and further investigation. 

Thanks for the discussion.
